summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive 3D web tool that helps mission planners pick where and when to land on the Moon and where they then want to drive. For any site and any date it will take the NASA grade ephemeris and work out when the Sun and Earth are above the horizon. That gives the planner the length of time the lander has power, the length of time it has a direct Earth link and the length of its longest night.

A HorizonNet machine learning model predicts the local horizon for every pixel of a lunar terrain model. It can be run on real NASA LOLA elevation data that you load in (which tells you which areas are lit and which are in contact). A decision model then ranks the scenarios using hard constraints, TOPSIS scoring and a robustness test over random weightings. A traverse planner then finds rover routes that keep the rover powered and in contact.

Everything is on a 3D globe with the landing sites and routes and you've got a local 3D terrain view with real Sun shadows.

It's important as polar missions are all about light and communications. You can now compare site and date options in seconds rather than hours.
details:
What it does and how it works

Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a browser app for comparing lunar landing sites and dates and planning rover traverses. You create scenarios (a site and a landing date for each). For each scenario the app uses the ephemeris from the astronomy engine and the IAU lunar rotation model (with libration) to work out the Sun and Earth positions at that site. It then reports the sunlit time, Earth visibility, the longest night and the longest comms outage.

HorizonNet is a small U-Net with 212,472 parameters. It predicts the local horizon in 16 directions for every pixel of a terrain model and runs completely in JavaScript in the browser. You can drop in a real NASA LOLA elevation GeoTIFF and it will turn that into a 100m per pixel, 12.8km terrain model. The predicted horizons show you which locations are lit and which are in contact with the Earth.

A decision model with hard constraints and TOPSIS scoring. It then randomly varies the criterion weights 1,500 times to see how often each scenario comes out on top. A traverse planner will find rover routes that take into account sunlight, Earth link and slope, all under a hard slope constraint. It will compare the smart route to the shortest route.

Everything is displayed on a 3D globe with the landing sites and routes and on a local 3D terrain view which is lit by the real Sun with shadows.

Benefits

Planners can compare site and date options in seconds within a single tool rather than having to jump between disparate ones. Nothing needs installing and there is no backend. Scenarios can be shared via link.

Intended impact

The objective is to get to site selection and re-planning faster and more transparently if the launch does get delayed. It should also make lunar illumination and communications a bit easier to understand for the students and the public.

Tools, languages and software

JavaScript, React 18, Vite, three.js, astronomy-engine and geotiff (for reading NASA GeoTIFFs). Trained in JAX in Python (using NumPy and SciPy) on CPU. Exported as raw weights and run in plain JavaScript. Code is checked against the original model, physics against astronomy-engine and Apollo 11. Interface tested in headless Chromium with Playwright and the site is deployed on Vercel. No special hardware required.

Creativity

It's all in one tool really: a 3D mission console, an ML horizon model and a decision model. It takes terrain, light and comms and puts them all into one comparison, with the routes actually on the 3D Moon. Nothing is hidden from view. The app will tell you whether a given result is based on real NASA terrain or on the inbuilt synthetic terrain.

Factors we considered

Accuracy: the physics is checked against independent sources.

Honest limits: the model that's been shipped was trained on synthetic terrain and so won't necessarily generalise to real terrain. The validation sheet does a comparison against exact ray-cast (which is ground truth on a real elevation model). Scripts for retraining on real LOLA tiles are included. A JPL Horizons cross-check has not yet been done.

Validation against NASA maps: the NASA illumination products have different scaling and averaging periods so we report the correlation and calibrated error rather than the raw differences.

Access is simple really, no accounts required, no servers required. If NASA’s online imagery is down it just falls back to the bundled map.
dataRefs: NASA Moon Trek (LRO WAC global mosaic imagery, loaded live as the globe texture)
NASA LRO LOLA lunar elevation data (loaded as GeoTIFF terrain models)
NASA LRO LOLA illumination and Earth-visibility products (used for validation)
NASA Apollo landing-site coordinates (Apollo 11 used to check the Sun-elevation calculation)
